title: Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm
subtitle: Permissive hypotension, CT if it responds, EVAR first if it fits

sources.title: ESVS 2024 Clinical Practice Guidelines on the Management of Abdominal Aorto-Iliac Artery Aneurysms
The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm
Endovascular or open repair strategy for ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm: 30 day outcomes from IMPROVE randomised trial (BMJ)

red_flags.text: Collapse or syncope with abdominal, back or flank pain in anyone over about 50, especially a male smoker. This is a rupture until proven otherwise.
A known aneurysm with new pain, even with normal observations. A symptomatic intact aneurysm is an urgent repair, not an outpatient review.
Shock that responds briefly to fluid and then recurs: the retroperitoneum has stopped containing the bleed.
Renal colic, diverticulitis or a 'muscular back' diagnosed for the first time in an older vasculopath. These are the classic misdiagnoses.
Loss of consciousness or cardiac arrest before repair. Outcome is very poor and the decision to operate must be made by a senior.

do_now.text: Call the on-call vascular surgeon, anaesthetist and theatre at the first suspicion. Do not wait for imaging to make the call.
Two large-bore cannulae, crossmatch, activate the major haemorrhage protocol. Do not place an arterial or central line if it delays transfer to CT or theatre.
Permissive hypotension: accept a low systolic pressure while the patient is conscious and talking. Give blood products rather than crystalloid, and avoid fluid boluses aimed at a normal pressure.
Aim for a door-to-intervention time under 90 minutes. Every unnecessary step before theatre is time the retroperitoneum may not give you.
Do not induce general anaesthesia outside theatre. Induction removes sympathetic tone and abdominal wall tamponade, and can precipitate arrest.

assess.text: Conscious level is the best bedside measure of perfusion here. A talking patient with a low pressure is perfusing their brain.
Palpate for an expansile mass, but its absence does not exclude rupture, particularly in an obese or distended abdomen.
Ask about prior aneurysm surveillance, previous EVAR or open repair, and anticoagulants. A previous repair raises endoleak, graft infection and aorto-enteric fistula.
Assess frailty and premorbid function quickly, and look for an advance decision. These shape whether repair is offered at all.
Check the groins and legs for pulses and mottling: limb ischaemia and access vessel size both matter for EVAR.

investigate.text: Bedside ultrasound confirms an aneurysm but cannot exclude rupture. Its role is to make the call, not to make the diagnosis.
CT angiography in the patient who is stable or responding to resuscitation. It confirms rupture and decides whether the anatomy suits EVAR.
Group and crossmatch, FBC, coagulation, fibrinogen, U&E, venous or arterial gas with lactate. Viscoelastic testing where available.
The unstable patient who does not respond goes straight to theatre. CT in that patient is a scan on the way to the mortuary.

resuscitate.text: Haemostatic resuscitation with blood and products per the major haemorrhage protocol. Correct fibrinogen and calcium, and keep the patient warm.
Consider EVAR under local anaesthesia with sedation kept to a minimum. In IMPROVE, local anaesthesia was associated with lower mortality.
In refractory shock, a percutaneous aortic occlusion balloon placed via the femoral or brachial route can buy time for repair.
Prepare and drape the abdomen and both groins before induction for open repair, with the surgeon scrubbed and ready to clamp.

definitive.text: Endovascular repair is the first choice for a ruptured aneurysm with suitable anatomy, in centres that can offer it around the clock.
Open repair when the anatomy does not suit EVAR, or when an endovascular service is not available within a safe time.

An endovascular-first strategy did not reduce 30-day mortality versus open repair in IMPROVE, but gave earlier discharge and was cost-effective. Choose the repair the team can deliver fastest and best.
After either repair, monitor intra-abdominal pressure. Abdominal compartment syndrome is common after rupture and needs decompressive laparotomy.
Where repair is judged futile, offer good palliative care with the family present. This is a legitimate and kind outcome, not a failure.

escalate.text: Consultant vascular surgeon and consultant anaesthetist for every rupture, including the decision not to operate.
If there is no vascular service on site, transfer to the nearest centre that can repair a rupture, after senior-to-senior discussion. Do not delay transfer for CT if the receiving centre will scan.
Interventional radiology and the hybrid theatre team at the same call as theatre, so EVAR is not delayed by a second call.
Critical care bed for every survivor. Plan it before the patient leaves theatre.

notes: The pressure that keeps the patient talking is the right pressure. Chasing a normal number with crystalloid dilutes clotting and blows the clot off the hole.
Ultrasound tells you there is an aneurysm. The clinical picture tells you it has ruptured. CT tells you how to fix it, if there is time.
Most deaths from rupture happen before hospital. The ones you see have already been selected by a contained bleed: do not waste that.
